meta.name: Syncope on Warfarin — Occult GI Hemorrhage and the High-Risk Refusal

patient.name: Marjorie Halvorsen
patient.chiefComplaint: Fainted during the hymn at church and went down in the pew. She is awake now, insists she is fine, and wants to go home.

history.hpi: 72-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation on warfarin who lost consciousness while standing for a hymn during the 10:00 service. Witnesses say she went pale, her knees buckled, and she went down into the pew — she was out for perhaps 15 to 20 seconds, with no shaking, no incontinence, and no confusion afterward. She struck her right shoulder on the pew arm on the way down but did not hit her head. She is now awake, fully oriented, embarrassed by the attention, and adamant that she just stood up too fast. What she does not volunteer, and what only emerges on direct questioning, is that she has had a dull, gnawing epigastric ache for two days, has felt 'wrung out and weak' since yesterday, and passed a black, tarry, foul-smelling stool this morning that she dismissed as 'my iron pills, or something I ate.' She has not taken iron in years. She has been taking ibuprofen two or three times a day for the past week and a half for a sore shoulder — on top of warfarin. She lives alone. Her husband died four years ago and her daughter is two hours away in Milwaukee.
pastMedical: Atrial fibrillation — anticoagulated on warfarin for stroke prevention
Prior peptic ulcer disease approximately 15 years ago, treated and resolved
Lives alone; no cognitive impairment, fully independent
medications: Warfarin 5 mg PO daily — last INR check was 'a while ago, maybe two months?'
Ibuprofen 400 mg PO 2–3 times daily for the past 10 days (self-medicating a sore shoulder) — NSAID on top of warfarin
No iron supplement despite what she says
history.lastOralIntake: Tea and toast about 2 hours ago. Poor appetite for two days.
history.events: Two days of dull epigastric ache and progressive weakness. One black, tarry stool this morning. Ten days of daily NSAID use while anticoagulated on warfarin. Syncope while standing for a hymn; 15–20 seconds of unconsciousness, witnessed, no seizure activity, no head strike. Awake and oriented on EMS arrival and actively refusing transport.

scene.dispatch: Dispatch: 72-year-old female, syncopal episode at a church. Caller reports she fainted during the service, is awake now but 'looks a bit pale.' Conscious and breathing.
scene.location: Crowded church foyer. Patient has been helped to a folding chair near the coat racks. Service has let out and the foyer is full of people trying to help and getting in the way.
scene.safety: Scene safe but crowded and noisy — a dozen well-meaning parishioners are pressing in, and a private history is nearly impossible in this foyer. Move her to the ambulance or a side room early; you will not get the melena out of her with fifteen neighbors listening.
scene.bystanders: Several church members witnessed the event and confirm 15–20 seconds of unconsciousness, no shaking, no incontinence, and no head strike. A friend, Eleanor, mentions unprompted that Marjorie 'hasn't looked right all week' and 'didn't come to Thursday's coffee, which she never misses.' Her daughter is two hours away and reachable by phone.
visualCues: Elderly woman sitting upright in a folding chair, straightening her cardigan, visibly embarrassed
Skin is pale, cool, and dry — conjunctivae look washed-out when you pull the lower lid down
She is alert, articulate, and oriented ×4 — she will pass any capacity screen you give her
Right shoulder held stiffly from striking the pew arm; no head injury
Purse open on her lap with a warfarin bottle and a large bottle of ibuprofen sitting side by side
She keeps saying she is fine and glancing toward the parking lot and her car
Crowded, noisy foyer — no privacy for a history that involves her stool

phases.name: Initial Contact
phases.description: This is the most dangerous patient a crew will meet all shift, and she is going to smile at them and ask them to leave. She is A&O×4, her vitals look unremarkable, and she has a perfectly plausible story — she stood up too fast during a hymn. Every instinct says vasovagal, sign the refusal, clear the call. Here is what MATC actually says. The Syncope guideline's Review of Systems has a line item for OCCULT BLOOD LOSS (GI/GU), and its list of high-risk causes of syncope names GI BLEED explicitly under hemorrhagic. Its Additional Evaluation is not optional: cardiac monitoring, SpO2, ongoing vitals, 12-lead EKG, and a blood glucose. And its Key Consideration 2 is the sentence that governs this whole call — decisions about delayed or non-transport are for patients where a LOWER-RISK etiology is suspected, and they are made in consultation with medical direction. Nothing about a 72-year-old anticoagulated woman who syncopes is low-risk. The crew's job in this phase is to do the workup the protocol demands and to ask the questions that make her stop being reassuring — because she will not offer the melena. Someone has to ask.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Patent, speaking in full clear sentences
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Pulse 96 and IRREGULARLY IRREGULAR — she is in atrial fibrillation; radial pulse is present but soft; cap refill 3 sec

skin.color: pale — conjunctivae and nail beds notably washed out

clinicalPresentation.motorFunction: Symmetric and intact; no focal deficit; stroke screen negative; right shoulder tender from the pew but neurovascularly intact
otherFindings: SHE WILL PASS ANY CAPACITY SCREEN — A&O×4, articulate, no cognitive impairment. That is not the same as being safe to leave.
Vitals look 'fine' — that is what COMPENSATED hemorrhagic shock looks like in a beta-blocked patient
She is on METOPROLOL — her heart rate CANNOT rise to compensate. The tachycardia you are waiting for may never come.
Pale + cool + washed-out conjunctivae + soft pulse = poor perfusion hiding behind a normal number
Rhythm is atrial fibrillation — the reason she is anticoagulated in the first place
MELENA WILL NOT BE VOLUNTEERED. You have to ask about stool, directly, in private.
Warfarin + 10 days of daily NSAIDs = a GI bleed engine
MATC Syncope names GI BLEED as a HIGH-RISK hemorrhagic cause of syncope
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: Oh, this is all so silly. I just got a little lightheaded when I stood up for the hymn. I'm fine now, really — I just want to go home. Please don't make a fuss.

expectedActions.shortAction: ASK about occult blood loss (GI/GU) directly and in private — she will not volunteer the melena
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Syncope Review of Systems — 'occult blood loss (gastrointestinal (GI)/genitourinary (GU))' is a required line item in the syncope history, alongside medications, fluid losses, and palpitations. It is written into the protocol precisely because patients do not raise it. This one question, asked out of earshot of the foyer, is what converts a 'vasovagal old lady' into a hemorrhaging one.
expectedActions.protocolReference: MATC: Adult and Pediatric Syncope and Near Syncope
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Review of Systems: Current medications (new medications, changes in doses); Fluid losses (nausea/vomiting/diarrhea) and fluid intake; Last menstrual period/pregnant; Occult blood loss (gastrointestinal (GI)/genitourinary (GU)); Palpitations; Unilateral Leg swelling, history of recent travel, prolonged immobilization, malignancy.

expectedActions.shortAction: Do the required syncope workup: cardiac monitor, SpO2, 12-lead EKG, BGL, ongoing vitals
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Syncope Pertinent Physical Exam / Additional Evaluation — cardiac monitoring, oxygen saturation, ongoing vital signs, 12-lead EKG, and blood glucose are the named evaluation set for ANY syncope patient. Acquisition of a 12-lead and application of a cardiac monitor are the protocol's two stated performance measures. This is not a workup the crew gets to skip because the patient looks well and wants to leave.
expectedActions.protocolReference: MATC: Adult and Pediatric Syncope and Near Syncope
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Pertinent Physical Exam: Additional Evaluation: Cardiac monitoring; Oxygen saturation (SPO2); Ongoing vital signs; 12-lead EKG; Blood glucose level (BGL). Performance Measures: Acquisition of 12-lead EKG. Application of cardiac monitor.

expectedActions.shortAction: Evaluate for hemorrhage and treat for shock if indicated; establish IV access
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Syncope Treatment 1 — treatment is directed at abnormalities discovered on exam and explicitly includes 'evaluate for hemorrhage and treat for shock if indicated,' establishing IV access, and a fluid bolus if appropriate. Her pallor, cool skin, and soft pulse are the abnormalities; the protocol tells the crew what to do about them.
expectedActions.protocolReference: MATC: Adult and Pediatric Syncope and Near Syncope
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Treatment and Interventions: Should be directed at abnormalities discovered in the physical exam or on additional examination and may include management of cardiac dysrhythmias, cardiac ischemia/infarct, hemorrhage, shock, etc.: Manage airway as indicated; Oxygen as appropriate; Evaluate for hemorrhage and treat for shock if indicated; Establish IV access; Fluid bolus if appropriate; Cardiac monitor; 12-lead EKG; Monitor for and treat arrhythmias.

expectedActions.shortAction: Recognize compensated shock behind 'normal' vitals — she is beta-blocked and cannot mount a tachycardia
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Shock Inclusion Criteria 1 — signs of poor perfusion include delayed capillary refill greater than 3 seconds, cool skin, and weak/decreased pulses, ANY ONE of which qualifies. Educational Pearl 4 adds that hypotension indicates UNCOMPENSATED shock — meaning a normal blood pressure never excluded shock in the first place. Her metoprolol blunts the compensatory tachycardia, so the crew must read perfusion, not pulse rate.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Signs of poor perfusion (due to a medical cause) such as one or more of the following: Altered mental status; Delayed capillary refill (> 3 seconds); Decreased urine output; Hypotension for age (lowest acceptable systolic blood pressure in mmHg): Greater than 10 years old: 90; Tachycardia or bradycardia for age; Weak, decreased or bounding pulses; Cool/mottled or flushed/ruddy skin. Hypotension indicates uncompensated shock, which may progress to cardiopulmonary failure within minutes.

expectedActions.shortAction: Screen the fall for trauma — geriatric patients falling from standing sustain significant injury
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Syncope Patient Safety 2 — geriatric patients suffering falls from standing may sustain significant injury and should be diligently screened for trauma. She struck her shoulder on the pew arm. On warfarin, even an unimpressive mechanism deserves a real secondary exam, and a head strike would change the entire disposition.
expectedActions.protocolReference: MATC: Adult and Pediatric Syncope and Near Syncope
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Patient Safety Considerations: Patients suffering from syncope due to arrhythmia may experience recurrent arrhythmias and should therefore be placed on a cardiac monitor. Geriatric patients suffering falls from standing may sustain significant injury and should be diligently screened for trauma.

expectedActions.shortAction: Move her out of the crowded foyer — you will not get a stool history with 15 neighbors listening
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Syncope Review of Systems requires asking about occult GI/GU blood loss, and MATC Abdominal Pain Key Documentation requires assessment of the abdomen. Neither is obtainable in a church lobby full of parishioners. Getting the history the protocol demands requires creating the conditions in which it can be given.
expectedActions.protocolReference: MATC: Adult and Pediatric Syncope and Near Syncope
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Review of Systems: Occult blood loss (gastrointestinal (GI)/genitourinary (GU)). Pertinent Physical Exam: Attention to vital signs and evaluation for trauma. Note overall patient appearance, diaphoresis, pallor. Heart, lung, abdominal, and extremity exam.

transitions.if: Occult blood loss asked; melena revealed
transitions.condition: Crew moves her somewhere private, completes the syncope workup, and asks directly about stool and bleeding. She admits to two days of epigastric ache, profound weakness, and a black tarry stool this morning — and to ten days of daily ibuprofen on top of her warfarin.

transitions.if: Refusal accepted; no workup, no med control
transitions.condition: Crew accepts 'I stood up too fast,' performs no 12-lead or monitor, never asks about occult blood loss, never contacts medical direction, and has her sign a refusal. She walks to her car and syncopes again in the parking lot — this time striking her head on the pavement while fully anticoagulated.

phases.name: Melena revealed; she still refuses
phases.description: The crew asked, and the picture inverts. Two days of gnawing epigastric pain. Profound weakness since yesterday. A black, tarry, foul-smelling stool this morning that she rationalized as iron pills she does not take. And ten days of daily ibuprofen layered on top of warfarin — an NSAID stripping her gastric mucosa while an anticoagulant guarantees that whatever it opens will not close. This is an upper GI hemorrhage in a fully anticoagulated 72-year-old, and MATC's Abdominal Pain guideline flags it in one sentence: abdominal pain in older adults, patients with bleeding disorders, and patients on anticoagulation medications may be a harbinger for severe illness. Her repeat pressure has slipped and her pulse has climbed as far as a beta-blocked heart can take it. AND SHE STILL SAYS NO. She is competent, she understands the words, and she is still going to walk to her car. This is where the protocol stops being about medicine and becomes about disposition: MATC's Syncope guideline authorizes delayed or non-transport ONLY where a LOWER-RISK etiology is suspected, and ONLY in consultation with medical direction. GI bleed is on the protocol's high-risk list by name. The crew cannot make this decision alone, and the protocol never asked them to.
phases.triggerCondition: Direct questioning revealed melena this morning, two days of epigastric pain, progressive weakness, and 10 days of daily NSAID use on top of warfarin. Repeat vitals show a widening compensation gap. The patient continues to refuse transport.

clinicalPresentation.circulation: Pulse 108, irregularly irregular; radial pulse softer than on arrival; cap refill 4 sec

skin.color: notably pale — conjunctival pallor now obvious

clinicalPresentation.motorFunction: Symmetric, but she is visibly weaker — needs help to stand and admits it
otherFindings: MELENA this morning + 2 days epigastric pain + weakness = UPPER GI HEMORRHAGE
WARFARIN + 10 days of daily NSAIDs — the NSAID opens the ulcer, the warfarin keeps it open
MATC Abdominal Pain: anticoagulated older adults with abdominal pain = 'harbinger for severe illness'
MATC Syncope: GI BLEED is named on the HIGH-RISK hemorrhagic causes list
BP 104/62 (was 116/70); HR 108 (was 96); cap refill 4 sec — the compensation gap is widening
She is beta-blocked — her heart rate is near the ceiling of what it can do. Do not wait for 130.
SHE IS COMPETENT AND SHE IS STILL REFUSING — this is now a disposition problem, not a clinical one
MATC gates non-transport to LOWER-RISK etiologies AND consultation with medical direction. She is neither.
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: I've had that before, it's just my iron pills or something. I am not going to the hospital today. I've got a roast in the oven and I feel perfectly well enough to drive myself home.

expectedActions.shortAction: Name the risk: anticoagulated older adult with abdominal pain = harbinger of severe illness
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Abdominal Pain Patient Safety Considerations — abdominal pain in older adults, patients with bleeding disorders, patients on anticoagulation medications, children under 2, and the immunocompromised may be a harbinger for severe illness. She is two of those categories at once. This sentence is the protocol's explicit warning against treating her presentation as benign.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Patient Safety Considerations: Abdominal pain in older adults, patients with bleeding disorders, patients on anticoagulation medications, children less than 2 years old and patients that are immunocompromised may be a harbinger for severe illness. Pertinent Assessment Findings: Rectal bleeding, hematemesis, vaginal bleeding.

expectedActions.shortAction: GI bleed is a named HIGH-RISK cause of syncope — this is not vasovagal
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Syncope Key Consideration 3 — the high-risk causes of syncope are enumerated, and GI bleed sits under Hemorrhagic alongside ruptured ectopic pregnancy and aortic rupture. The moment melena is disclosed, this patient moves onto that list by name, and every downstream decision — including whether non-transport is even on the table — changes with her.
expectedActions.protocolReference: MATC: Adult and Pediatric Syncope and Near Syncope
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: High-risk causes of syncope include, but are not limited to, the following: Cardiovascular: Myocardial infarction; Aortic stenosis; Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy; Pulmonary embolus; Aortic dissection; Dysrhythmia. Neurovascular: Intracranial hemorrhage; Transient ischemic attack or stroke. Hemorrhagic: Ruptured ectopic pregnancy; GI bleed; Aortic rupture.

expectedActions.shortAction: Contact online medical direction — non-transport requires consultation, and this is NOT low-risk
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Syncope Key Consideration 2 — decisions regarding delayed or non-transport should be made in consultation with medical direction, and the protocol scopes that pathway to patients 'where a LOWER risk etiology is suspected, e.g., vasovagal syncope.' She is on the high-risk list. The crew is not authorized to clear this refusal on their own judgment, and the physician is a resource the protocol actively directs them to use — including letting the physician speak with her directly.
expectedActions.protocolReference: MATC: Adult and Pediatric Syncope and Near Syncope
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Key Considerations: By being most proximate to the scene and to the patient's presentation, EMS clinicians are commonly in a unique position to identify the cause of syncope. For patients where a lower risk etiology is suspected, e.g., vasovagal syncope, decisions regarding delayed or non-transport should be made in consultation with medical direction.

expectedActions.shortAction: IV access (2 attempts or 90 sec → IO); fluid bolus titrated to MAP 65; EtCO2 <25 = poor perfusion
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Shock Treatment 4, 8, and 9 — establish access with the 90-second/two-attempt rule, monitor EtCO2 (under 25 mmHg suggests poor perfusion — hers is drifting down at 32), and give pressure-infused boluses targeting an adult MAP of 65. She is bleeding into her gut and she is going to need volume whether she consents to the hospital or not.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Pulse oximetry and EtCO2 (reading of less than 25 mmHg may be sign of poor perfusion). Establish IV access. If unable to obtain within two attempts or less than 90 seconds, place an IO needle. IV fluid volume goal attained by giving boluses that are pressure infused over less than 15 minutes each based on patient's condition and clinical impression. Adult: Physiologic target: MAP goal 65 mmHg. Fluid goal of up to 30 mL/kg of isotonic fluid by administering rapid, predetermined boluses (e.g., 500 mL) unless the MAP goal is achieved, or pulmonary edema develops.

expectedActions.shortAction: Serial vitals q5 min and DOCUMENT the trend — the trend is the argument
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Shock Key Documentation Elements — full vital signs with reassessment every 15 minutes or more frequently as appropriate. MATC Syncope Key Documentation adds presenting rhythm, BP, pulse, and whether the patient is recovered or still symptomatic. For a refusing patient, the documented downward trend is simultaneously the clinical picture, the persuasive evidence to show her, and the crew's legal record.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Key Documentation Elements: Medications administered. Full vital signs (pulse, blood pressure, respiratory rate, neurologic status assessment) with reassessment q 15 minutes or more frequently as appropriate. Lactate level (if available). Neurologic status assessment. Amount of fluids given.

expectedActions.shortAction: Advance notification: anticoagulated GI bleed with syncope — they will need reversal and endoscopy
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Shock Treatment 13 — provide advanced notification to the hospital. An anticoagulated upper GI bleed needs the receiving team mobilizing reversal agents, blood products, and GI before she rolls through the door, not after.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Provide advanced notification to the hospital. Performance Measures: Percentage of patients with suspected shock for whom advanced notification to the hospital was provided. Mean time from abnormal vitals to initiation of a fluid bolus.

transitions.condition: Crew contacts online medical direction, presents a concise report, and the physician speaks directly with the patient. Confronted with the trend in her own vitals and a physician's voice, she consents to transport. IV access is established, fluids are started, and she is transported with advance notification.

phases.name: Med control consulted; transport accepted
phases.description: The physician on the radio said the words the crew could not make land: you are bleeding internally, your blood thinner means it will not stop on its own, and if you go home you may not wake up. She agreed to go. She is on the monitor in atrial fibrillation, has two lines, and is receiving fluid titrated to a MAP of 65 while the crew watches her EtCO2 as a perfusion tracer. Note what actually saved this patient — not a drug, not a procedure. Someone asked about her stool. Someone did a 12-lead she said she did not need. Someone called a physician instead of accepting a signature. MATC's Syncope guideline says EMS clinicians, by being most proximate to the scene and the presentation, are commonly in a unique position to identify the cause of syncope. That is exactly what happened here, and it happened because the crew treated a well-appearing woman as a hemorrhage patient on the strength of one question.
phases.triggerCondition: Online medical direction consulted; physician spoke directly with the patient. She consented to transport. IV access established, fluid resuscitation titrated to MAP 65, continuous monitoring and advance notification en route.

clinicalPresentation.circulation: Pulse 100, irregularly irregular; radial pulse improving with fluid; cap refill 3 sec

skin.color: still pale but no longer worsening

otherFindings: Two large-bore IVs; isotonic fluid titrated to MAP 65 (not to a number she 'looks like' she needs)
EtCO2 back up to 35 with fluid — a useful perfusion tracer in occult hemorrhage
Continuous monitor: atrial fibrillation, rate-controlled, no new arrhythmia
Advance notification given: anticoagulated upper GI bleed with syncope — reversal agents and GI needed
WHAT SAVED HER: a question about her stool, a 12-lead she said she didn't need, and a phone call instead of a signature
She is still hemorrhaging. The fluid is a bridge; endoscopy and reversal are the fix.
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: (quietly) The doctor said I could have bled to death in my sleep. I really didn't think it was anything. I just thought I stood up too fast.

expectedActions.shortAction: Titrate isotonic fluid to MAP 65 — boluses pressure-infused over <15 min, reassess after each
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Shock Treatment 9a — the adult physiologic target is a MAP of 65 mmHg, achieved with rapid predetermined boluses (e.g., 500 mL) pressure-infused over less than 15 minutes, reassessing after each. MAP is calculated as [(2 × diastolic) + systolic] / 3 — a number the crew should be computing, not eyeballing.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: IV fluid volume goal attained by giving boluses that are pressure infused over less than 15 minutes each based on patient's condition and clinical impression. Fluid volume goal to achieve a mean arterial pressure (adults) or other targets (pediatrics). Mean Arterial Pressure is calculated: (MAP = [(2X diastolic) + (systolic]/3). Adult: Physiologic target: MAP goal 65 mmHg. Fluid goal of up to 30 mL/kg of isotonic fluid by administering rapid, predetermined boluses (e.g., 500 mL) unless the MAP goal is achieved.

expectedActions.shortAction: Keep her on the monitor — recurrent arrhythmia is a live risk in syncope
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Syncope Patient Safety 1 — patients suffering syncope due to arrhythmia may experience recurrent arrhythmias and should therefore be placed on a cardiac monitor. She is in atrial fibrillation and is being volume-resuscitated; the monitor stays on through transport.
expectedActions.protocolReference: MATC: Adult and Pediatric Syncope and Near Syncope
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Patient Safety Considerations: Patients suffering from syncope due to arrhythmia may experience recurrent arrhythmias and should therefore be placed on a cardiac monitor. Key Documentation Elements: Presenting cardiac rhythm. Cardiac rhythm present when patient is symptomatic. Any cardiac rhythm changes.

expectedActions.shortAction: Watch for decompensation — falling EtCO2, rising cap refill, mentation change
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Shock Educational Pearl 4 and Treatment 4 — hypotension indicates UNCOMPENSATED shock which may progress to cardiopulmonary failure within minutes, and an EtCO2 under 25 mmHg may be a sign of poor perfusion. In an actively bleeding patient, the compensation she has been running on can fail abruptly and without much warning.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Hypotension indicates uncompensated shock, which may progress to cardiopulmonary failure within minutes. In most adults, tachycardia is the first sign of compensated shock, and may persist for hours. Pulse oximetry and EtCO2 (reading of less than 25 mmHg may be sign of poor perfusion).

expectedActions.shortAction: Handoff: syncope + melena + warfarin + NSAIDs + trend — give them the reasoning, not just numbers
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Syncope Key Documentation Elements — symptoms immediately preceding the event, patient status on EMS arrival, presenting rhythm, and rhythm changes. MATC Shock Documentation adds the medication list and fluid totals. The ED needs the NSAID-plus-warfarin mechanism to understand why they are about to reverse her.
expectedActions.protocolReference: MATC: Adult and Pediatric Syncope and Near Syncope
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Key Documentation Elements: Presenting cardiac rhythm; Cardiac rhythm present when patient is symptomatic; Any cardiac rhythm changes; Blood pressure; Pulse; Blood glucose level (BGL); Symptoms immediately preceding event; Patient status on EMS arrival: recovered or still symptomatic.

phases.name: Refusal accepted; no workup, no med control
phases.description: The crew took the easy story. No 12-lead, no monitor, no question about her stool, no call to medical direction — just a signature on a refusal form and a well-appearing 72-year-old walking out to her car. She made it about forty feet across the parking lot before her second syncopal episode, and this time there was no pew to catch her. She struck the back of her head on the asphalt. She is now a fully anticoagulated patient with a head injury and an ongoing GI hemorrhage, which is roughly the worst combination in geriatric prehospital medicine: warfarin means an intracranial bleed does not tamponade, and the GI bleed means she has no reserve to lose. She is GCS 12 and dropping, hypotensive at 82/48, with a boggy occipital hematoma. Everything the crew skipped is now mandatory, and it is being done in a parking lot with a worse patient. Note the honest part of this failure: she had capacity. She could have refused even a perfect crew. But a perfect crew would have done the workup, found the melena, called a physician, and documented all of it — and the protocol says that is what non-transport requires.
phases.triggerCondition: Refusal accepted without the required syncope workup, without asking about occult blood loss, and without consulting medical direction. The patient syncopized again in the parking lot and struck her head while fully anticoagulated.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Patent but at risk — she is drowsy and her gag is sluggish
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Pulse 118, irregularly irregular, weak and thready; cap refill 5 sec
clinicalPresentation.pupils: Equal at 3 mm but SLUGGISH — recheck them with any further decline
clinicalPresentation.motorFunction: Moves all four but weakly; no lateralizing signs YET
otherFindings: SECOND SYNCOPE — head strike on asphalt, boggy occipital hematoma, no helmet of any kind
FULLY ANTICOAGULATED HEAD INJURY: warfarin means an intracranial bleed will not tamponade itself
PLUS an ongoing GI hemorrhage — she has no reserve to give to a second bleed
GCS 12 and drifting — MATC classifies GCS 9–13 as MODERATE head injury
SBP 82 — head injury target for an adult is SBP ≥ 110. She is 28 mmHg below it.
Hypotension after head injury is the single most preventable cause of secondary brain injury
She HAD capacity and could have refused a perfect crew — but a perfect crew would have done the workup, found the melena, and called a physician
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: (drowsy, slurred) …hit my head… I'm so tired…

expectedActions.shortAction: Maintain SBP ≥110 — give fluid to PREVENT hypotension, do not wait until she is already hypotensive
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Head Injury Treatment 3b and 3c — for adults over 10 years, maintain SBP greater than or equal to 110 mmHg, and administer NS/LR boluses to maintain SBP above threshold. The protocol is emphatic: do not wait until after the patient is already hypotensive — PREVENT hypotension. She is at 82. Hypotension is the most powerful driver of secondary brain injury available to the crew, and it is the one they control.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Circulation: Moderate/severe closed head injury: Blood pressure: avoid hypotension: Adult (age greater than 10 years): maintain SBP greater than or equal to 110 mmHg. Closed head injury: Administer normal saline (NS)/lactated Ringer's (LR) fluid boluses to maintain SBP above threshold. Do not wait until after the patient is already hypotensive—prevent hypotension.

expectedActions.shortAction: High-flow O2 via NRB as a precaution against unanticipated deterioration
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Head Injury Treatment 1a — administer high-flow oxygen via non-rebreather as a precaution against unanticipated deterioration. Patient Care Goal 1a is to promote adequate oxygenation and preoxygenate against exactly the deterioration this anticoagulated patient is at high risk of.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Airway: Administer high-flow oxygen via NRB (non-rebreather) as a precaution against unanticipated deterioration. Patient Care Goals: Limit disability and mortality from head injury by limiting secondary brain injury through promoting adequate oxygenation and preoxygenating to protect against unanticipated deterioration; Promoting good cerebral perfusion and avoid hypotension; Preventing hypocapnia (by avoiding hyperventilation and overventilation).

expectedActions.shortAction: Do NOT hyperventilate — maintain EtCO2 35–45; hypocapnia worsens secondary brain injury
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Head Injury Patient Safety 1 and Key Consideration 4 — maintain all patients in an EtCO2 range of 35–45 mmHg. Hyperventilation causes cerebral vasoconstriction, which further decreases blood flow to an injured brain and worsens the secondary injury. Her EtCO2 is already 27 from poor perfusion; bagging her faster makes it worse in both directions.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Patient Safety Considerations: Do not hyperventilate patients: Maintain all patients in EtCO2 range of 35–45 mmHg. Assume concomitant cervical spine injury in patients with moderate/severe head injury. Key Considerations: Herniation is difficult to diagnose in the prehospital setting. Hyperventilation results in vasoconstriction which further decreases blood flow to the brain and worsens the secondary brain injury.

expectedActions.shortAction: Assume c-spine injury — moderate head injury with altered mental status; collar her
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Head Injury Patient Safety 2 — assume concomitant cervical spine injury in patients with moderate/severe head injury. She is GCS 12 (moderate) after an unwitnessed-mechanism fall onto pavement from standing height.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Patient Safety Considerations: Assume concomitant cervical spine injury in patients with moderate/severe head injury. Assessment: Maintain cervical stabilization. Geriatric Consideration: Elderly patients with ankylosing spondylitis or severe kyphosis should be padded and immobilized in a position of comfort and may not tolerate a cervical collar.

expectedActions.shortAction: Preferential transport to the highest level of trauma care — GCS 3–13 meets the criterion
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Head Injury Treatment 5a — preferential transport to the highest level of care within the trauma system for GCS 3–13, or P/U on the AVPU scale. She is GCS 12. An anticoagulated intracranial bleed needs a CT scanner and a neurosurgeon, and the community hospital cannot reverse what it cannot see.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Transport destination specific to head trauma: Preferential transport to highest level of care within trauma system: GCS 3–13, P (pain) or U (unresponsive) on AVPU scale; Penetrating head trauma; Open or depressed skull fracture.

expectedActions.shortAction: Trend GCS and pupils — recheck pupils with ANY decrease in mentation
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Head Injury Assessment 3c and Treatment 4c — perform and trend the neurologic status assessment, and reassess pupils with any decrease in mentation. Early signs of deterioration are confusion, agitation, drowsiness, vomiting, and severe headache. In an anticoagulated bleed, the interval between 'drowsy' and 'herniating' can be very short.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Perform and trend neurologic status assessment (GCS or AVPU scale): Early signs of deterioration: Confusion; Agitation; Drowsiness; Vomiting; Severe headache. Eyes: Evaluate pupil size and reaction to light to establish baseline; Reassess pupils if decrease in mentation.

expectedActions.shortAction: Do not forget the GI bleed — she is hemorrhaging from two places now; fluid targets BOTH
expectedActions.rationale: MATC Shock Treatment 9 and Head Injury Treatment 3c — the shock protocol's MAP 65 target and the head injury protocol's SBP 110 target are BOTH in play, and the higher one governs. The original occult GI hemorrhage never stopped; it is now the reason she cannot hold the pressure her injured brain requires.
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: IV fluid volume goal attained by giving boluses that are pressure infused over less than 15 minutes each based on patient's condition and clinical impression. Adult: Physiologic target: MAP goal 65 mmHg. Fluid goal of up to 30 mL/kg of isotonic fluid by administering rapid, predetermined boluses (e.g., 500 mL) unless the MAP goal is achieved, or pulmonary edema develops.
